pairs.rationale: Both opening notices refer to composing an account. Luke mentions multiple prior undertakings concerning fulfilled events; Acts addresses its own prior account of Jesus' deeds and teaching. This is a literary-preface comparison, not a claim that Acts identifies every account Luke mentions.

Both connect testimony with people present from the beginning. Luke describes transmitted eyewitness testimony and service of the word; John records Jesus telling the disciples that they testify because they have been with Him from the beginning.

Both address Theophilus in connection with a written account. Luke describes careful investigation and an orderly account; Acts refers to the first account about Jesus. The connection uses the linked addressee-and-account context rather than a loose match of a personal name alone.

Both writers explain their writing as enabling readers to know something with confidence. Luke concerns certainty about received instruction; John concerns believers knowing they have eternal life. The subject matter and intended assurance are not treated as identical.

Luke identifies Zechariah with the priestly division of Abijah; Chronicles lists Abia as the eighth priestly allotment in its surrounding division list. The name forms remain as supplied, and this does not identify Zechariah with an unrelated prophet of the same name.

Both describe blamelessness in relation to observance of the law. Luke praises the couple's conduct in the Lord's commandments and ordinances; Paul describes his own former standing concerning righteousness in law. The persons and the surrounding arguments differ.

Both describe a marriage without children because the wife is barren. Genesis names Sara; Luke names Elizabeth and additionally specifies the couple's advanced age. The two couples are not identified as one.

Luke's priest serving in his division corresponds to the ordered priestly ministry entering the Lord's house described in Chronicles. Chronicles supplies institutional background, not a report of Zechariah's particular service.

Exodus prescribes the priestly burning of incense before the Lord morning and evening. Luke narrates Zechariah's incense duty in the sanctuary; the Exodus passage does not establish Luke's separate lot-selection detail.

Both associate prayer with incense before God. Luke describes people actually praying during the incense hour; the psalm likens prayer to incense and raised hands to evening sacrifice. It does not describe Luke's crowd or fix its hour.

Both birth-announcement settings begin with an angel of the Lord appearing before the promise of a child. Judges addresses a barren woman; Luke addresses the priest Zechariah by the incense altar. Judges does not supply the altar or its right-hand position.

This same-book comparison links fear at an angelic appearance in two infancy scenes. Zechariah fears when he sees the angel; the shepherds fear at the angel and surrounding glory. The people and scenes remain distinct.

Both announce that a named wife will bear a son and give the child's name in advance. God names Isaac for Abraham and Sarah; Luke's angel names John for Zechariah and Elizabeth. The promises and children are not conflated.

This same-chapter promise of rejoicing at John's birth corresponds to the later account of Elizabeth's neighbors and relatives rejoicing with her. It is an internal promise-and-narrative link, not independent attestation of the birth.

John's prohibition on wine and strong drink recalls Hannah's vow that her promised son will drink neither wine nor intoxicating drink in the supplied Saints Samuel text. Samuel also mentions no iron on the head; Luke does not add that restriction or explicitly call John a Nazirite. Luke's Holy-Spirit statement is additional.

Luke predicts John's turning many Israelites toward the Lord; Acts recalls John's proclamation of a baptism of repentance to all Israel before Jesus' arrival. The later ministry notice supplies a concrete counterpart to the preparatory mission, without quoting every word of the prediction.

Luke describes John going in Elijah's spirit and power and turning fathers' hearts toward children. Saints Malachi announces Elijah and restoration of a father's heart toward a son and a person's heart toward a neighbor. The different second relationships are preserved, and John is not declared literally the historical Elijah.

Both men respond to a promised birth by raising the problem of advanced parental age. Abraham laughs and names his and Sarah's ages; Zechariah asks how he will know and describes himself and his wife as old. Their reactions and the later divine responses are not made identical.

Both name Gabriel in a divine communication. Daniel hears a voice commissioning Gabriel to explain a vision; Luke has Gabriel identify himself and his mission to announce good news. Daniel's verse does not state Luke's description of standing before God.

Both describe a divinely governed period of inability to speak followed by an opening of the mouth. Luke makes Zechariah's silence a response to unbelief until the announced events occur; Ezekiel's silence and later speech concern a different prophetic commission and an embittering house.

Both vision settings involve silence and subsequent communication. Luke explicitly says Zechariah cannot speak and makes signs; Daniel falls silent and then opens his mouth after a touch to his lips. The comparison does not assign the same cause or duration to their silence.

Both narrate conception in fulfillment of a preceding promise concerning an elderly couple. Genesis describes the Lord's promised visitation to Sarah and her conception; Luke describes Elizabeth conceiving and adds five months of seclusion, which Genesis does not reproduce.

Elizabeth's statement about God removing disgrace recalls Rachel's declaration that God has taken away her reproach after conceiving and bearing a son. The women and births are distinct, and the supplied disgrace/reproach wording is retained.

This same-chapter connection identifies Gabriel as the envoy previously introduced to Zechariah. The later sending to Nazareth begins a distinct announcement to Mary; the earlier self-introduction does not independently establish the sixth month or destination.

Both connect Mary with betrothal to Joseph, and Matthew's angel addresses Joseph as son of David alongside Luke's identification of his Davidic house. Matthew narrates an already discovered pregnancy; Luke introduces the virgin before the announcement. The different narrative stages remain distinct.

Both angelic greetings assure the person addressed that the Lord is with them. Luke greets Mary as favored; Judges addresses Gideon as a mighty man of strength. The recipients and commissions are different.

This same-chapter comparison links the troubled responses to the two angelic appearances. Mary is troubled by the saying and considers the greeting; Zechariah is troubled on seeing the angel and fears. The distinct causes of the reactions are preserved.

Both announcements begin with the angel telling the named recipient not to fear. Mary's assurance concerns grace found with God; Zechariah's concerns his heard petition and Elizabeth's promised son. This is a repeated same-chapter annunciation pattern, not one announcement.
Both announce Mary's bearing a Son and direct that He be named Jesus. Luke addresses Mary before conception; Matthew's angel addresses Joseph and adds salvation from sins as the naming explanation.

Luke's promise of David's throne recalls God's promise to David concerning his seed, the prepared kingdom and a throne established forever. The Samuel verses supply the royal promise, not Luke's exact title Son of the Most High.

Both promise an enduring royal house or kingdom and throne. Luke applies an unending reign to Mary's Son over Jacob's house; Samuel speaks of the royal house and kingdom in the Davidic promise. The named houses are not silently made the same expression.

Both identify conception in the absence of the prior marital relations at issue. Mary asks prospectively because she does not know a man; Matthew narrates pregnancy before Mary and Joseph came together. The question and the narrated discovery occur at different stages.

Both attribute Mary's conception to the Holy Spirit. Luke's angel explains it to Mary with overshadowing and Son-of-God language; Matthew's angel explains the already conceived child to Joseph without repeating those additional phrases.

Both describe a son conceived or born in an elderly couple's fulfillment of promise. Luke names Elizabeth as Mary's relative and specifies the sixth month; Genesis names Sarah and Abraham and does not supply those relational or timing details.

Both insist on the efficacy of God's word in the setting of a surprising promised birth. Genesis asks whether any word is impossible with God and names Sarah's future son; Luke says no word from God will be powerless. The births and question/assertion forms differ.

Both speakers accept God's promise in the language of His servant and ask for the spoken word to be made effective. Mary consents to the announcement about her Son; David asks confirmation of the word concerning his servant and house. These are different responses to different promises.

Both describe movement of children in a mother's womb. Rebekah's children leap within her and prompt her troubled question; Elizabeth's infant leaps at Mary's greeting, with Elizabeth later interpreting the movement as joy. The pregnancies and meanings of the movements differ.

Elizabeth's blessing of Mary among women recalls the blessing of Jael among women in Deborah's song. Luke additionally blesses the fruit of Mary's womb; Judges praises Jael in a different setting and does not assign her Mary's maternal role.

Elizabeth asks how the mother of her Lord should come to her, recalling David's question about how the Lord's ark will come to him. This is a possible verbal visitation allusion across distinct narratives; it does not explicitly identify Mary as the ark or equate the surrounding events.

This internal narrative-and-speech connection links the narrated leap at Mary's greeting with Elizabeth's explanation that the infant leaped with gladness when she heard it. The second account adds the expressed interpretation of joy; it is not an independent witness report.

Both associate believing God's promise with a remarkable conception. Elizabeth blesses Mary's belief in fulfillment of the Lord's words; Hebrews describes Sarah's faith in the faithful One who promised. The women, promises and circumstances are distinct.

Mary's soul magnifying the Lord recalls the psalm's call to magnify the Lord and exalt His name together. The psalm invites shared praise; Mary begins her own song. This is shared worship language, not an explicit quotation attribution.
Mary's rejoicing in God her Savior recalls Hannah's rejoicing in the Lord's salvation. Both maternal songs praise God, while the speakers and the occasions of their songs differ.

Mary's praise that God looked upon His servant's lowly condition recalls Hannah's request that the Lord look upon His servant's humiliation. Hannah petitions for a child; Mary praises grace already announced and adds future generations calling her blessed.

Both praise God's holy name in connection with His mighty or saving action. Mary names the Mighty One's great deeds for her; the psalm names redemption for His people and His commanded covenant. It does not describe Mary's personal experience.

Both speak of the Lord's enduring mercy toward those who fear Him across generations. Luke says generations and generations; the psalm says from eternity to eternity and additionally speaks of righteousness for children's children.

Both join the Lord's mighty arm with the defeat or scattering of opposing pride. Luke speaks of scattering the proud in their heart's thought; the psalm describes humbling a proud one and scattering enemies with the arm of power. The objects and imagery are not silently made identical.

Both songs describe the Lord lowering and raising people in a reversal of status. Luke mentions rulers brought from thrones and lowly people raised; Hannah's song mentions humbling, exalting and raising the poor to sit with rulers on a throne. The examples differ.

Both praise God for filling hungry people with good things. Luke pairs that action with the rich being sent away empty; the psalm's paired description concerns an empty soul and a hungry soul, not Luke's rich.

Both connect remembered divine mercy with Israel. Luke describes helping Israel His servant; the psalm describes the Lord remembering mercy to Jacob and truth to Israel's house and adds the earth seeing His salvation.

Both connect God's mercy or promise to Abraham with what was spoken or sworn to the fathers. Luke mentions Abraham and his offspring forever; Micah names mercy to Abraham, truth to Jacob and the ancient oath. The differing clauses remain distinct.

The birth of Elizabeth's son fulfills the angel's earlier same-chapter announcement that Elizabeth would bear Zechariah a son. The name commanded in the promise is addressed in the subsequent naming scene.

The relatives' and neighbors' rejoicing with Elizabeth provides the same-chapter narrative counterpart to the promise that many would rejoice at John's birth. Luke also interprets the event as the Lord magnifying mercy toward Elizabeth.
Luke's eighth-day circumcision corresponds to the eighth-day circumcision prescribed in Leviticus. The law does not prescribe the proposed name Zechariah or narrate this particular naming gathering.

Elizabeth's insistence that the child be called John agrees with the angel's prior command to give that name. This internal link does not assert how Elizabeth learned the command, which the cited verses do not explain.

Both parts of the same narrative use signs during Zechariah's inability to speak. Earlier Zechariah makes signs to the people; at the naming others make signs to him. The gestures alone are not treated as proof that he was deaf.

Zechariah's written declaration that the child's name is John follows the name prescribed by the angel earlier in the same chapter. It is an internal naming-fulfillment connection, with the later wonder of the observers additional.

Zechariah's restored speech at the naming resolves the same-chapter announcement that he would be unable to speak until the promised events occurred. The later verse adds his blessing God rather than repeating the angel's rebuke.

Both scenes combine fear after a remarkable divine action with a report spreading through a region. Here the account concerns John's birth and Zechariah's restored speech; Luke 7 concerns Jesus raising a widow's son and the people's declaration of God's visitation. They are different events.

Both use the Lord's hand being with a person or group to indicate divine aid. Luke concerns the child's future; Acts concerns people proclaiming the Lord Jesus and many believing. The common expression does not identify John with those later missionaries.

Both connect the Holy Spirit with prophetic speech. Zechariah is filled and prophesies; Acts describes the Spirit coming upon people after Paul's laying on hands, followed by tongues and prophecy. The recipients and accompanying actions differ.

Zechariah praises the Lord for accomplishing redemption for His people; the psalm says He sent redemption to His people. Luke adds visitation and the blessing of Israel's God, while the psalm adds the commanded covenant and God's holy name.

Luke's horn of salvation in David's house recalls the Lord causing a horn to spring up for David in the psalm. Luke adds salvation and the raising-up statement; the psalm also describes a lamp for the anointed. This royal image is not used to make the Aaronic child John a Davidic heir.

Both speak of God speaking through the mouth of His holy prophets from long ago. Zechariah introduces promised salvation; Acts speaks of restoration and heaven's reception of Jesus. The shared prophetic formula does not collapse the differing surrounding statements.

Both speak of salvation from the hand of those who hate God's people and redemption or rescue from enemies. The psalm recalls deliverance at the sea in its context; Zechariah speaks prophetically of salvation without naming all those enemies as Egypt.

Both associate remembered covenant with divine mercy toward God's people. Luke refers to mercy to the fathers and the holy covenant; the psalm describes remembering His covenant and relenting according to abundant mercy during the people's distress.

Luke recalls the oath God swore to Abraham; Genesis supplies God's oath by Himself and His blessing and offspring promise to Abraham. The rescue-and-service wording continuing Luke's sentence is not presented as a verbatim part of Genesis' oath.

Both link deliverance of God's people with subsequent service to God. Exodus promises that Moses and the people brought from Egypt will serve God on the mountain; Luke speaks of rescue from enemies to serve without fear. The enemies and settings are not identified as the same.

Both join holiness and righteousness in the life oriented to God. Luke describes ongoing service before Him; Ephesians describes putting on the new person created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. This is an ethical-language comparison, not the same argument.

Zechariah says the child will go before the Lord to prepare His ways; Malachi announces a messenger who will look to a way before God's face in the supplied wording. Luke assigns John a preparatory role and adds prophet of the Most High, without identifying him with every messenger figure in Malachi's verse.

This same-book link connects Zechariah's prediction concerning salvation in forgiveness with the later ministry of John explicitly identified as Zechariah's son. John proclaims a baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins; the later passage supplies the public ministry, not every phrase of the prediction.

Luke's dawn from on high visiting through God's mercy recalls Malachi's rising sun of righteousness with healing. This is a proposed light-and-rising image allusion, not an explicit quotation; Luke does not reproduce Malachi's healing wings or its audience description.

Both describe light reaching people in darkness and death's shadow. Isaiah speaks of a great light shining on the people walking or dwelling there; Luke adds the directing of feet into peace. The added peace clause is not claimed as a quotation of this verse.

The same-book childhood summaries both describe a child growing and becoming strong. John grows strong in spirit and remains in the wilderness until his manifestation to Israel; Jesus is described with wisdom and God's grace. These are deliberately distinguished children and developmental summaries.

deferred.reason: The crowd's waiting and wondering at the priest's delay is distinctive narrative detail; no sufficiently specific independent counterpart was retained.
Completing the period of priestly duty and returning home is a narrative transition; a generic service or return passage would add little.
The haste, hill-country journey and unnamed city of Judah do not justify identifying a particular city or equating another journey.
Entering Zechariah's house and greeting Elizabeth is a distinctive narrative transition; later verses already give the meaningful response to the greeting.

The approximate three-month stay and return home have no sufficiently specific retained counterpart. No inference is made that Mary remained for John's birth or that a separate three-month stay establishes an identity.
The relatives' statement that no one in the family has this name has no defensible independent counterpart; shared personal names would not establish family identity.

review_notes: Every one of Luke 1's 80 saved original source units is represented once as a paired source or a deferred source; source wording is not edited.

Internal narrative links are labeled as same-book or same-chapter connections and are not independent attestations. Similar birth settings and hymnic language do not identify distinct mothers, children or events.

Targets follow the Saints saved original numbering, including Greek-Old-Testament Psalm and Malachi divisions. Differing titles, images, audiences and narrative circumstances are retained in the rationales.

Read all 80 source units and every retained target with surrounding context; 74 distinct source units have 74 retained pairs and 6 are deferred. Original target ID existence, original-order contiguity, duplicate pairs, self-target exclusions and all-source coverage were checked.
